the temperature-induced bending vibrations in the CO₂ molecule are responsible for the appearance of the quadrupole-allowed excitations in the valence electron spectrum of CO2 at high momentum transfer.

In summary, our research is concerned with
a detailed study of the temperature dependence of CO2 valence excitations in a wide range of momentum transfers.
the temperature dependence of CO2 valence excitations in the dipole and higher multipole regimes and the interplay between temperature- and momentum-transfer-induced nondipolar effects.
the interplay between temperature- and momentum-transfer-induced effects in the valance excitations of CO2.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the temperature-activated vibrations in CO2 are a source of nondipole effects in the valance excitations, which are particularly important at higher momentum transfers.
the temperature-induced excitation spectrum of the CO₂ is a superposition of the temperature-independent dipole-allowed spectrum and the temperature-dependent dipole-forbidden spectrum.
, in addition to the dipole and nondipole effects, the temperature dependence of valence excitations is governed by temperature-activated bending vibrations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the dipole and the nondipole contributions to the X-ray absorption and emission spectra are not additive, as the nondipole effects are strongly dependent on the temperature of the sample and on the momentum transfer.
temperature-induced bending mode vibrations in the CO₂ molecule are a major contributor to the nondipolar excitations in the valence region.
the dipole- and quadrupole-level simulations are able to reproduce the experimental data, but only when the temperature-activated vibrations are included.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dipole-forbidden excitation spectra of CO2 can be measured in the dipole regime by exploiting temperature-activated vibrations.
temperature-induced vibrations and finite momentum transfer have to be considered simultaneously to understand the valence exciton spectrum of CO2.
the interplay of temperature-activated vibrational modes and higher-multipole effects can be used to extract the nondipole contributions to the valence excitation spectra.
